catalog_quote: El iñapari es un idioma tonal restringido. Es decir, en esta lengua el tono de la voz juega un papel limitado en la función comunicativa. Raras veces sirve para distinguir ítems léxicos como en el ticuna, ni tampoco funciona en el sistema gramatical como en el bora. Más bien, tiene el efecto culminativo de delimitar las palabras dentro de la cadena hablada. Entre los sustantivos y los adjetivos, cada palabra normalmente tiene un solo tono alto, aunque algunas palabras tienen dos. Salvo en el caso de algunas palabras bi-silábicas, el tono alto no suele caer en la primera sílaba de la palabra; esta sílaba, al igual que todas las sílabas que le siguen al tono alto, llevan un tono bajo. Así que lo más correcto sería clasificar el iñapari como una lengua de tono-acento (pitch-accent), igual que el nomatsiguenga. Aunque la ubicación del acento o tono alto en determinadas palabras es mayormente impredecible, hemos encontrado muy pocos casos de pares mínimos distinguidos solamente por el tono o acento. Un ejemplo sería el contraste entre [anáwa] 'ellos' y [anawá] 'canoa'. Damos a continuación algunos ejemplos que muestran dos tonos altos en vez de uno solo: (25) [iwáná] 'río' [iyábítʸa] 'su corteza (de un árbol)' [aáwíri] 'flor' [itehétíro] 'amiga; compañera' [ipúʔúri] 'pueblo; lugar'

new_statements.translation: Iñapari is a restricted tone language. [...] Among nouns and adjectives, each word normally has a single high tone, although some words have two. Except in the case of some disyllabic words, the high tone does not usually fall on the first syllable of the word; that syllable, like all the syllables that follow the high tone, bears low tone. So the most correct thing would be to classify Iñapari as a pitch-accent language, like Nomatsiguenga. Although the location of the accent or high tone in particular words is mostly unpredictable, we have found very few minimal pairs distinguished solely by tone or accent.
new_statements.citation: Parker, Stephen G. (comp.) 1995. Datos de la lengua iñapari. Documento de Trabajo 27. Yarinacocha: Ministerio de Educación / Instituto Lingüístico de Verano.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: The quotation was checked again. Es decir, en esta lengua el tono de la voz juega un papel limitado en la función comunicativa.') and continues on p. 18 exactly as quoted: 'Raras veces sirve para distinguir ítems léxicos como en el ticuna, ni tampoco funciona en el sistema gramatical como en el bora. Más bien, tiene el efecto culminativo de delimitar las palabras dentro de la cadena hablada. Entre los sustantivos y los adjetivos, cada pala…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Culminative pitch accent: each (nominal/adjectival) word carries one high-toned syllable (occasionally two), whose position is lexically specified and 'mostly unpredictable'; it rarely falls on the word-initial syllable except in some disyllables, and every syllable after the H is low. Accent is marked with an acute on every entry in the vocabulary. Minimal pairs exist but are rare (anáwa 'they' vs anawá 'canoe').
new_statements.secondary_stress: No secondary stress described; some words carry two high tones (e.g. [iwáná] 'río', [aáwíri] 'flor'), and the two moras of a long vowel may differ in tone ([mapaá] 'colmena').
new_statements.exceptions: Some disyllables have H on the first syllable; a few words have two H tones; §4.1 sandhi: (i) the final low tone of many verb forms surfaces as high when another word follows within the phonological phrase (unless the next word begins with H); (ii) an underlying H on the second syllable of a disyllabic word is delinked when the preceding word ends in H (never applies to H on a first syllable or to words of three or more syllables).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level (culminative, 'delimits words in the speech chain'); statement made for nouns and adjectives in citation form, with verbs discussed via phrase-level tone sandhi. Author frames the system as restricted tone / pitch accent rather than stress. Data from the last fluent speakers (one family, río Piedras, Madre de Dios, fieldwork 1993-94).
new_statements.identity_note: Source describes Iñapari (inap1242, ISO inp) as spoken by the last family of speakers on the río Piedras, Madre de Dios, Peru (Parker fieldwork 1993-94); no dialect distinction. SAPhon spells the page 'Inyapari'.

new_statements.quote: Word stress is lexically contrastive in Iñapari. [...] Stress overwhelmingly occurs on the penultimate syllable in many elicited lexical items in my data. Consequently, I only indicate stress if it is not on the penultimate syllable. Acoustically, word stress appears to be associated with changes in intensity (and perhaps also pitch). [p. 95] [...] Tone is acoustically, and solely, correlated with changes in pitch in Iñapari; only a high pitch has been recorded. Moreover, this pitch is associated with some bound morphemes, regardless of word stress [p. 96] [...] I cannot offer a more detailed description of tone or stress at this point [p. 97]. (fn. 2, p. 88: Every Iñapari word has one prominent syllable.)
new_statements.citation: Rogers, Chris. 2021. Salient morphosyntactic patterns of Iñapari. Language Documentation and Description 20: 86-122.
new_statements.locator: Sec. 2.3 'Stress and tone', pp. 95-97 (PDF pp. 11-13); also fn. 2, p. 88 (PDF p. 4)
new_statements.check: confirmed by a second reader, with minor differences
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (the PDF's metadata: 38 pp., native text layer, 1248224 bytes; Internet Archive copy of elpublishing.org/docs/1/20/). Sec. 2.3 'Stress and tone' is doc pp. 95-97 = PDF pp. 11-13 as stated. All quoted sentences are present verbatim: p. 95 'Word stress is lexically contrastive in Iñapari.' followed by ex. (16) anáʋa 'they' / anaʋá 'canoe', ʔuʔá 'nest' / ʔúʔa 'woodpecker', háma 'to hear' / hamá 'tapir'; p. 95 'Stress overwhelmingly occurs on the penultimate syllable in many elicited lexical items in my data. Consequently, I only indicate stress if it is not on the penultimate syllable. Acoustically, word stress appears to be associated with changes in intensity (and perhaps also pitch).…
new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record has no rule; the existing statement (Parker 1995, sec. 4 'El tono') calls Iñapari a restricted tone language with one high tone per word, normally not on the first syllable, read as pitch accent. Rogers describes the same culminative prominence (one prominent syllable per word) but analyses it as lexically contrastive word STRESS cued by intensity, overwhelmingly penultimate, and separates it from a morpheme-bound high TONE cued by pitch alone. The placements are compatible (penultimate default; for disyllables Parker also allows the H on the first syllable), but the type differs: stress + restricted morphemic tone (Rogers) vs a single-H restricted tone / pitch accent sys…
new_statements.rule_in_words: One prominent syllable per word; stress is lexically contrastive (minimal pairs anáʋa 'they' / anaʋá 'canoe', ʔuʔá 'nest' / ʔúʔa 'woodpecker', háma 'to hear' / hamá 'tapir', ex. 16), with penultimate position as the overwhelming default in elicited lexical items, so only non-penultimate stress is marked. Stress is cued by intensity (perhaps also pitch). Separately, a high tone (pitch only) is bound to certain morphemes (-yíí contrastive focus, tʃií 'land') independently of word stress, and stress and tone can co-occur in one word.
new_statements.exceptions: (1) Polarity-question intonation moves stress to the final syllable regardless of its lexical position (no-niʔa-má-ri 'I eat it' vs no-niʔa-ma-rí 'Did I eat it?'), which Rogers takes to be sentential/phrasal stress. (2) Some bound morphemes carry fixed stress that always takes primary word stress, e.g. causative -ʔá (n-eta-ʔá-ma-ri 'I found him'). (3) Some morphemes carry a high tone independent of stress.
new_statements.identity_note: Rogers 2021 describes the Iñapari of four sibling speakers in Sabaluyoc on the Las Piedras River, Madre de Dios, Peru (2019 fieldwork); Parker 1995 is SIL data from the same community's older generation. No dialect split is claimed.

new_statements.quote: As stated in point (f) above, among monomorphemic words (most of which are nouns), normally only one mora/syllable bears a high tone in the unmarked case; all other syllables receive a default low tone. Furthermore, the location in which these high tones occur is for the most part unpredictable (especially in nouns). As the term high tone implies, the primary physical correlate of this suprasegmental feature is relatively high pitch, but greater loudness or amplitude also accompanies these "accented" syllables. [...] For these reasons I feel most comfortable categorizing the tonal system of Iñapari as being "pitch-accent" in nature.
new_statements.citation: Parker, Steve. 1999. A Sketch of Iñapari Phonology. International Journal of American Linguistics 65(1): 1-39.

new_statements.relation_note: Same author and same data as the Parker 1995 existing statement ('idioma tonal restringido', H placement mostly unpredictable, first syllable normally not H) — this is the English, fuller analysis and agrees with it, adding the explicit 'pitch accent' classification, phonotactic constraints (a)-(g), the default penultimate accent under suffixation, alternating quantity-insensitive secondary stress, and an autosegmental single-H analysis. Relative to the catalog record classification tonal (world-2026-09-17, no rule): compatible but Parker explicitly hedges ('one might be inclined to conclude that Iñapari is not really a tonal language at all.. accentual or stress system'; settles on pitch a…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Iñapari has a restricted two-register (H/L) system that Parker classifies as pitch accent: most monomorphemic words carry a single high tone (some 2-4 H on adjacent moras), whose location is largely lexically unpredictable and contrastive (minimal pairs e.g. /anawa/ 'they' vs 'canoe', p. 18). Constraints (pp. 16-17): every word has at least one H and one L; tautomorphemic H tones must be adjacent (no HLH within a morpheme); in words of 3+ syllables the first syllable is never H; word-final H is very marked; at least one of the last four syllables must be H. There is also a 'default accent': under suffixation the H often shifts or spreads to the penultimate syllable of the derived word (pp. 20-22), though this is 'at most a preferred tendency or default option, not an absolute requirement' (p. 22). Correlates: high pitch plus greater loudness; final H realized as a fall in isolation.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Yes, predictable and rhythmic: 'secondary stresses do predictably fall on [even-num]bered syllables preceding each primary stress' (p. 14, PDF 15), i.e. 'predictable secondary stresses which propagate backward from a primary stress (high tone) on alternating syllables' (pp. 22-23); if the accent is far enough left a secondary stress may also follow it (p. 24). 'there is no evidence that the tone or accent system of Iñapari is quantity sensitive' — alternating stresses skip over long (geminate, tautosyllabic) vowels (pp. 24-25). Fn. 14: primary stress (accent) and secondary stress are governed by different principles.
new_statements.exceptions: Disyllables may have initial H (only word size allowing it); words ending in long vowels (e.g. /api:/ 'coati') may end in H; monomorphemic /iwana/ 'river' ends HH; multimorphemic words may have non-adjacent H tones; the last-four-syllables constraint holds only on the surface (te-coalescence cases, p. 19); penult shift/spread fails in e.g. /muyupiti/ 'finger', /mehiteapiti/ 'wing', /pamirina/ 'the others' (p. 22); two tonal sandhi processes affect verbs phrase-medially (p. 25ff).
new_statements.identity_note: Parker 1999 describes the same variety and speakers as Parker 1995 (the last Iñapari speakers on the Las Piedras river, Madre de Dios, Peru; data 'published in Parker 1995'); Rogers 2021 cites Glottolog inap1243 'Modern Iñapari', the dialect node under inap1242, same community. No dialect split among the sources.

readall_conflicts: Parker 1995 (existing statement, SIL data) treats the one-per-word prominence as a restricted high tone that normally avoids the first syllable and does not speak of stress; Rogers 2021 (2019 fieldwork) treats it as lexically contrastive word stress, overwhelmingly penultimate, realized by intensity (perhaps pitch), and posits in addition a separate morpheme-bound high tone realized by pitch alone. The descriptive placement facts are compatible (one culminative prominence per word, mostly penultimate, with lexical exceptions such as anaʋá 'canoe', hunoɾí 'rubber', and non-initial in longer words), but the two sources disagree on type (tone / pitch accent vs stress plus restricted tone). Rogers states his description of both stress and tone is preliminary. Parker 1999 (IJAL 65:1-39, the full phonology sketch) remains unopened (paywalled) and would be the source to settle.
